name: Namsoong at Namprikdang
when: Dec–Jan, the Lepcha new year (lunar, dates set each year)
summary: Namsoong is the Lepcha new year and harvest festival. Since 1979 its best-known public celebration has been held at Namprikdang, a riverside ground on the Teesta at the edge of Dzongu, with prayers, archery, traditional games, Lepcha food and dances.
body: Namsoong falls at the turn of the Lepcha year, in December or early January, at the same season as the Bhutia Losoong, and the state holiday is usually listed as Losoong/Namsoong. For Lepcha families it marks the end of the harvest and a time to honour local deities, mountains and rivers. The public festival at Namprikdang, near Mangan where the road crosses into Dzongu, has been organised since 1979, according to the Ministry of Tourism's Utsav festival listing.

A Namsoong day at Namprikdang usually opens with rituals and prayers for the coming year, then moves to competitions in traditional skills, archery being the favourite, along with games, music and folk dances in Lepcha dress. Food stalls sell Lepcha dishes, and chi, the fermented millet drink, is served in bamboo vessels. The Lepcha cultural bodies of Dzongu run the event, and outsiders are welcome as guests.

Namprikdang is a short drive from Mangan, so many visitors come for the day. Permit checks for festival day visitors have varied, so ask us; to sleep in a Dzongu homestay that week you need the usual Dzongu permit. Dates are fixed by the Lepcha calendar and announced locally, so check current status before you travel.
tips: Book a Dzongu homestay well ahead for Namsoong week, as Lepcha families host relatives too.
Ask before photographing rituals and elders, and do not step into the ritual area.
Carry cash in small notes for food stalls; card machines are rare at Namprikdang.

faqs.a: Namsoong follows the Lepcha calendar and usually falls in late December, close to the Bhutia Losoong, with celebrations running into early January. The Sikkim government announces the Losoong/Namsoong holiday each year, and the Namprikdang organisers announce their programme a few weeks ahead. Check current status before you travel, and ask us for the confirmed dates.

Namprikdang is a riverside ground at a Teesta confluence in Dzongu, a short drive from Mangan, the Mangan district headquarters. Mangan is about 67 km and 2.5–3 hours from Gangtok. The ground lies at a low altitude, below 1,000 m, so December days are mild, though mornings are cool.

faqs.q: Is Namsoong the same as Losoong?
faqs.a: They fall in the same season and share the idea of a harvest new year, which is why Sikkim lists the holiday as Losoong/Namsoong. Losoong is the Bhutia festival, marked with monastery masked dances at Phodong and Rumtek beforehand. Namsoong is the Lepcha celebration, with Lepcha rituals, archery, games and food, centred at Namprikdang in Dzongu.

faqs.q: Can tourists join the Namsoong festival?
faqs.a: Yes, visitors are welcome to watch and to eat at the stalls, and many Lepcha families are happy to explain what is happening. Dress modestly, follow the instructions of organisers, and ask before photographing people. If you want to stay inside Dzongu that week, you need a Dzongu permit and an early homestay booking.

name: Phodong Monastery Chaam
when: Usually early to mid December, 28th–29th day of the 10th Tibetan month (lunar)
summary: Phodong Monastery, a Karma Kagyu seat 38 km north of Gangtok, holds its annual masked dance on the 28th and 29th days of the 10th Tibetan month, usually in December. It is one of the Kagyed-season dances that lead up to the Losoong new year.
body: Phodong is one of the major monasteries of Sikkim, belonging to the Karma Kagyu school. The Mangan district administration credits its construction to Chogyal Gyurmed Namgyal in the 18th century, on the site of an older monastery. Every year, on the 28th and 29th days of the 10th month of the Tibetan calendar, its monks perform chaam, the sacred masked dance, in the monastery courtyard.

Chaam is a ritual, not a show. Monks in brocade robes and painted masks representing protector deities move in slow, exact steps to long horns, drums and cymbals, enacting the destruction of negative forces before the new year. Jesters appear between the serious dances to make the crowd laugh. In Sikkim these December dances are part of the Kagyed season that ends the year, and Wikipedia's Losoong article notes that the Losoong festival is preceded by masked dances at Phodong and Rumtek.

Phodong lies on the North Sikkim Highway, so the chaam is easy to reach on a day trip from Gangtok without a protected area permit for Indian travellers. Dates move with the lunar calendar. Check current status before you travel.
tips: Arrive by 9 am to find a place on the courtyard edge; locals fill it quickly.
Never cross the dance ground, and do not use flash or drones.
Combine the chaam with Labrang Monastery, 2 km uphill, and Kabi Lungchok on the way.

faqs.q: When is the Phodong chaam in 2026?
faqs.a: It falls on the 28th and 29th days of the 10th month of the Tibetan calendar, which usually lands in early to mid December. The exact Gregorian dates change each year with the lunar calendar. Check current status before you travel; we confirm dates with the monastery in November and can plan a Gangtok day trip around them.

faqs.q: Do I need a permit to see the Phodong chaam?
faqs.a: Indian travellers do not need a protected area permit for Phodong, which is on the North Sikkim Highway about 38 km and 1.5 hours from Gangtok. Foreign nationals need their Sikkim restricted area permit, applied online since January 2026, as for any visit to Sikkim. Rules change, so check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: What is the meaning of the masked dance at Phodong?
faqs.a: Chaam is a Buddhist ritual dance in which monks wearing masks of protector deities enact the overcoming of negative forces and obstacles before the new year. Each figure and step follows prescribed texts of the monastery's tradition. Jesters lighten the long ceremony. Watch quietly, as you would at any religious service.

faqs.q: What should I wear to the Phodong chaam in December?
faqs.a: Phodong sits at roughly 1,400–1,800 m, so December days are around 8–15 °C in the sun and cold in the shade of the courtyard. Wear warm layers, comfortable shoes and modest clothing covering shoulders and knees. Carry water, a cap and some cash for offerings and snacks sold outside the monastery.

name: Tholung Kamsel
when: Traditionally every three years, in spring; the 2021 Kamsel was held 23–26 November
summary: Every three years the sealed boxes of relics at Tholung Monastery in Upper Dzongu are opened, aired in the sun and shown to pilgrims. Kamsel (also spelled Kamsil or Khamsel) dates to the late 18th century and is overseen by Sikkim's Ecclesiastical Affairs Department.
body: Tholung Monastery, in remote Upper Dzongu inside the buffer zone of Khangchendzonga National Park, holds some of Sikkim's most precious religious objects. According to the monastery's history as summarised on Wikipedia, sacred manuscripts and relics from other monasteries were moved here for safety during the Gorkha invasions of the late 18th century, and the site was revealed as sacred in 1760 by the fourth Lhatsun, with a monastery built in 1789.

Tholung is cold and damp, so the objects, kept in more than a dozen sealed boxes, are taken out every three years to be aired and dried in the sun. The name Kamsel refers to this airing. Pilgrims come to see and receive blessings from items associated with Lhatsun Chenpo, the 17th-century lama revered as a founder of Buddhism in Sikkim, and other treasures.

The custom lapsed for nine years after the 2011 earthquake and a 2016 landslide cut access, and was revived from 23 to 26 November 2021, when EastMojo reported more than 6,000 devotees. Dates are set by the Ecclesiastical Affairs Department. Check current status before you travel.
tips: Pilgrims drive to the road head near Bey in Upper Dzongu, then walk 10–14 km through forest; allow 5–6 hours up.
You need a Dzongu permit and, as an outsider, should travel with a local guide or homestay host.
Carry rain gear, a torch, warm layers and your own water bottle; facilities on the trail are minimal.

faqs.q: When is the next Tholung Kamsel?
faqs.a: Kamsel is traditionally held every three years, but it has not always kept to schedule: it lapsed for nine years and was revived in November 2021. The Ecclesiastical Affairs Department of the Government of Sikkim decides the dates. We do not want to guess, so ask us and check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: How do I reach Tholung Monastery for Kamsel?
faqs.a: Drive from Mangan into Upper Dzongu to the road head near Bey, then walk. Sources give 10 to 14 km, with about 1,000 m of climb through dense forest, taking 5 to 6 hours. The monastery sits at about 2,400 m. Kamsel days bring hundreds of pilgrims, so homestays fill early.

faqs.q: What is shown during the Kamsel?
faqs.a: Sacred texts, ritual objects and personal belongings associated with Lhatsun Chenpo and other lamas are brought out of their sealed boxes, aired and shown to pilgrims, who receive blessings. A metal chorten at Tholung is said to hold the ashes of an incarnation of Lhatsun Chenpo. Photography rules are set by the monks: always ask.

faqs.q: Can tourists attend the Tholung Kamsel?
faqs.a: Respectful visitors can, provided they hold a Dzongu permit and come as pilgrims rather than sightseers. It is a religious occasion run by the state's ecclesiastical department and the monastery. Walk with a local guide, dress modestly, keep to the instructions of monks and volunteers, and carry your own food and water.
